beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Installing Software on an HPC Cluster. How to get software running on a shared cluster without root: modules, Conda, Spack and EasyBuild, source builds, and Apptainer containers, and which one to reach for first.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Jambo. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. On a shared cluster you do not install software the way you do on a laptop. There is no sudo, no root, no system package manager you are allowed to touch. Everything you install goes into your own space, built against the cluster's own libraries. This lecture walks the main ways to get research software running on a shared cluster: environment modules, Conda, Spack, EasyBuild, compiling from source with your own module files, and App-tainer containers. And then, which one to reach for first.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. Root: the administrator account that can write to system directories; you do not have it. A module: a package an administrator already built, loaded by name and version. User space: your home, scratch or project directories, the only places you can install. A build from source: compiling a program's code yourself, with your own options. A module file: the small text file that tells the module command what to change. And a container: an application packed with its whole operating system into one image file.

beats.narration_text: Why it is different. Your laptop: root access, one user, a local disk with no quota, and generic downloads that just work. The cluster: user space only, hundreds of people sharing the login node, a network filesystem with tight quotas, and builds that should link against the cluster's own compilers, M P I and math libraries. A generic binary from the internet ignores all of that, so it runs slower, or will not launch across nodes.

beats.narration_text: Two habits follow. First, do not build on the login node. Everyone who is connected shares it; a long compile or a memory-hungry install there slows the system for all of them. Heavy builds go into an interactive job or a batch job. Second, mind the filesystem. Your home directory is a network filesystem, N F S, G P F S or Lustre, shared across every node. Quotas are tight, and it is tuned for large reads, not the tens of thousands of tiny files a Conda environment or a build tree creates. That is a real reason job launches are slow.

beats.narration_text: Before installing anything, check whether it already exists. Most clusters expose preinstalled software through environment modules. This cluster uses the classic T C L based Environment Modules, not L mod, so a few commands differ from other tutorials. Module avail lists what is there; avail with a name filters it; show prints what a module would change; load adds it; list shows what is loaded; unload removes one; purge clears everything. Names and versions are cluster-specific, so always check avail first.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own commands and files land in order.

beats.narration_text: What module load actually does. It does not install anything. It edits your shell's environment, the PATH variable and its library cousin, so the shell can find a package an administrator built once and shares with everyone. Load a module and PATH gains the package directory in front of user bin. Unload it and the directory is gone. That is how you switch between versions cleanly, with no conflicts. And the fastest install is the one you do not have to do.

On 'module load python/3.11' (mono command lands above), a kraft pill 'package dir' slides in front of /usr/bin inside PATH and a GHOST arrow links it to the package box. On 'unload', the pill slides out. Then two version pills '3.11' and '3.13' swap in and out of the slot in turn.

beats.narration_text: Conda is where most researchers start, especially in Python and R. It installs into your own directory, handles non-Python libraries too, and needs no root. On most clusters you load a Conda module rather than installing Conda yourself. Create an environment with a Python version and packages, activate it with source activate, and check. Channels: prefer conda-forge, which has far broader and more current coverage, and remove the defaults channel. Anaconda's terms restrict large organisations' use of its default channels, and many universities now avoid them.

beats.narration_text: Now the pitfalls, the part people skip and then file a ticket about. Solving an environment is heavy, so do it in an interactive job, not on the login node. Watch your home quota: an environment is tens of thousands of small files. But do not put environments on scratch, because scratch is purged, and the environment vanishes, sometimes mid-project. Keep environments in persistent space, home or a project directory. The one piece you can safely send to scratch is the package cache, which is regenerable. Or just empty it now and then.

beats.narration_text: In your dot conda R C, redirect only the package cache to scratch. If home is tight, create environments at a path in a project directory with dash p. And activate inside the job script, never in dot bash R C. Conda's init command writes a block into dot bash R C that auto-activates on every login; it slows every login and can break batch jobs. Comment that block out.

beats.narration_text: The job script does the activating: load the Conda module, source activate, run. And for reproducibility, export the environment to a Y M L file, exact, with builds, and recreate it later from that file.

beats.narration_text: Spack is a package manager built for HPC. Unlike Conda, it builds from source by default, and it lets you choose the compiler, the M P I implementation and the build options, holding many versions side by side. One honest note first. Spack and EasyBuild are heavy: long compiles, big disk footprints, real upkeep. They are not the first thing to reach for. If a module or Conda covers you, use that. Spack's core idea is the spec: package, at version, percent compiler, plus variant. H D F five at one point fourteen point three, percent G C C twelve point two, plus M P I. Spack resolves the whole dependency tree and builds each piece with exactly those choices. The version numbers here are illustrative.

beats.narration_text: The workflow. Clone Spack, source its setup script to load it into your shell, list and info a package to see versions and variants, install it with the variant you want, and spack load it. A clean install with many dependencies compiles for a long time, so run spack install inside a job with several cores. A Spack environment groups specs for one project: create it, activate it, add specs, install everything, and commit the spack dot yaml it writes.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own commands and files land in order.

beats.narration_text: EasyBuild solves a similar problem with a different philosophy. It builds from recipe files called easyconfigs, and you almost never write one: thousands ship with it, so you install a package by name and the recipe is fixed, which is the reproducibility selling point. A toolchain is a named bundle of compiler, M P I and math libraries; gom-pee is G C C plus Open M P I. There is no EasyBuild module here, so you install it once into a Conda environment. Then search for a recipe and run E B with three flags that are easy to miss.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own commands and files land in order.

beats.narration_text: Those three flags. Modules tool equals Environment Modules, because EasyBuild assumes L mod by default and this cluster does not run it. Module syntax equals T C L, because Loo-ah module files will not load here. And install path in your own space, because you cannot write to system directories. Put them in a config file once. Then the key detail: EasyBuild's output is a module file. Point module at its directory with module use, and load the result with module load like any preinstalled package.

beats.narration_text: Spack versus EasyBuild, in four rows. How you install: a spec on the command line, versus a named recipe. Dependencies: Spack resolves a flexible graph; EasyBuild follows a fixed toolchain. Output: spack load or a module, versus always a module file. Strength: flexible variants and versions, versus strict, repeatable, toolchain-based builds. And the candid note from experience: neither is the recommended first option on this cluster. Both are heavy to set up and painful to maintain, and Spack in particular can be frustrating when builds break. Reach for them only when you need source-level control and have decided the upkeep is worth it.

beats.narration_text: Sometimes nothing prebuilt exists, or you need a patch, a specific version, or a flag no package manager exposes. Then you compile from source. The project's README or INSTALL file names its build system; the two you will meet most are Autotools, a configure script, and C make. Autotools: configure with a prefix, make with several cores, make install. C make: load the C make module, configure with an install prefix, build, install. Always read the project's own instructions first.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own commands and files land in order.

beats.narration_text: What makes it an HPC build. Always set a prefix; you cannot install to the system's user local directory. Load the cluster's compiler and libraries as modules before you configure, so the build links against the optimised versions; that is the same reason Spack and EasyBuild produce fast binaries. Point parallel or numerical code at the cluster's M P I and BLAS and LAPACK, not a slow generic fallback. And run the make step inside a job, because dash j eight is a multi-core workload. Five steps: load modules, configure with a prefix, compile inside a job, install into the prefix, expose it on PATH or with a module file.

A grey X lands on a '/usr/local' label at the start; an 'M P I · BLAS · LAPACK' library block links to station 3 with a GHOST line.

beats.narration_text: After installing to a prefix, the shell still does not know the software exists. Export PATH and L D library path by hand, and it works for this session. For something you reuse, write your own module file instead. Make a directory, tell module to look there with module use, in your dot bash R C, so it persists, and write the file. This cluster's module files are T C L. The first line, hash percent Module, must be exactly that, the magic cookie that marks the file as a module file. Two prepend-path lines, one for PATH and one for the library path, and a one-line description.
beats.motion_claim: The training's own commands and files land in order.

beats.narration_text: The directory name becomes the module name and the file name becomes the version. Now module avail shows your build, module load sets the paths for you, and unload reverses everything cleanly. One module file becomes a personal stack: each tool its own subdirectory, each version a file inside it, so my tool one point oh and two point oh sit side by side and you switch with one load, exactly like the cluster's compilers. A module file can load other modules, such as the right G C C, and a dot version file names the default.

beats.narration_text: App tainer, formerly Singularity, brings containers to HPC. A container packs an application with its entire operating system environment into a single image file, a dot S I F, so it runs the same way everywhere. Why not Docker? Docker normally needs root to run, a security problem on a shared system. App-tainer runs a container as you, with no elevated privileges, works with the scheduler and the shared filesystem, runs G P U and M P I workloads, and can pull and convert Docker images, so you are not locked out of that ecosystem.

beats.narration_text: App-tainer is installed system-wide, no module needed. Pull an existing image, including from Docker registries, into a dot S I F file. Exec runs one command inside it. Shell opens an interactive shell inside it. The dot S I F is one file: copy it, archive it, share it, and it reproduces the same environment.

beats.narration_text: To build your own, you describe the image in a definition file: bootstrap from a Docker image, Ubuntu twenty-two oh four; a post section that installs Python and numpy; and a runscript that says what runs by default.

beats.narration_text: Build images on your own machine, not on the cluster: building a dot S I F from scratch generally needs root. So build where you have it, your laptop or a workstation, then copy the finished image up with S C P and exec it on the cluster. The privileged step stays on a machine you control; only the unprivileged run happens here. Containers shine when software is hard to install natively, when a research group already publishes an image, or when you want one portable artifact to move between clusters or cite. The cost is image size and the upfront build.

beats.narration_text: Choosing the tool. Six options, and none needs root. Environment modules: preinstalled, best for what the cluster already provides, limited to what admins installed. Conda: prebuilt binaries, best for Python and R and quick setups, heavy on quota. Spack: builds from source, source-level control and many variants, heavy and slow to maintain. EasyBuild: from source, reproducible toolchain builds, mostly an admin tool, toolchain-bound. A source install: full control, patches and niche tools, the most manual and the easiest to get wrong. App-tainer: an image, for hard dependencies and portability, built locally then copied up.

beats.narration_text: Now, the practical order. One: check for a module first; the best install is no install. Two: a Python or R package? Conda, with the quota and login-node precautions. Three: isolated, portable, or a nightmare of dependencies? Build a container on your own machine and run it here. Four: a patch, a specific version, or a build flag nothing else exposes? Build from source. Five: source-level control over compiler, M P I or variants, and willing to maintain it? Then, and mostly then, Spack or EasyBuild. And if none of that fits, ask the Research Computing team.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. No root and a shared filesystem, so every install goes in your own space, off the login node, mindful of quota. Check for a module first; module load only edits your environment. Conda for Python and R: conda-forge, environments in persistent space, activate in the job script. Spack and EasyBuild build from source and are the heavy, advanced option, not the default.
